Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

vignette:
Javier is a 26-year-old Latino man who works as a maid at a mid-sized hotel chain in a Southern state. He lives alone, divorced for the past two years. His PCL-5 score of 73 reflects the severe, pervasive hold his trauma has on him.

The event that shattered his life happened five years ago in his home country. Javier had been active in a student group that advocated for land reform. One evening, as he walked home, a dark sedan-a common model, nothing distinctive-pulled up beside him. Two men in police uniforms stepped out, ordered him into the back seat, and drove him to a disused warehouse. Over the next three days they interrogated him, beat him, burned his arms with cigarettes, and used electrical shocks on his legs. Their methods alternated between brutality and feigned kindness: one torturer would bring him water, speak softly, and then tighten the restraints. That disorienting switch-a moment of relief that turned into more pain-left a deep confusion inside him. When he finally escaped during a transfer, he fled north, crossed the border, and was granted asylum. He has not returned.

Everyday life is a minefield. Javier sees dark sedans everywhere-in the hotel parking lot, outside the grocery store-and each one makes his chest tighten. He cannot watch news reports about his home country; the images of police or military convoys send him into a cold sweat. Most puzzling to him is the way positive emotions trigger a sinking dread. If he feels a moment of genuine happiness-a guest complimenting his work, a song he used to love-his mind instantly scans for the coming betrayal. He has come to believe that feeling good is a trap, a lull before pain. He cannot trust it.

To manage these intrusions, Javier has built a rigid life. He avoids being reminded of his past: if a coworker asks about his background, he changes the subject or walks away. He is especially wary of anyone in uniform or in a position of authority. His hotel manager wears a blazer and a badge, and Javier speaks to him only when absolutely necessary, keeping his eyes down. He has quit two previous jobs because a supervisor raised his voice once, and that was enough. He smokes a pack and a half a day now-the only thing that steadies his hands when the memories surge. He knows it hurts his lungs, but the alternative-the panic-is worse.

At night, he wakes repeatedly. He has a routine: right after he lies down, he gets up to check the door lock three times, then the window latch, then under the bed. Only then can he try to sleep, but he always jolts awake around 2 a.m., ears straining for footsteps. The slightest unexpected touch-a hand on his shoulder in a crowded hallway-makes him flinch violently, and he has embarrassed himself more than once by yelping or shoving a person back. He feels a constant, low-grade threat from strangers: anyone who approaches him on the street, even a lost tourist asking for directions, makes his pulse race and his gaze dart for an exit.

His marriage collapsed about a year after he arrived in the U.S. His wife, also an immigrant, tried to comfort him by rubbing his back one night. He spun around, shouting, and then spent the rest of the night on the floor, shaking. She could not understand why he kept pushing her away, why he could not let himself laugh at a movie, why every unexpected hug felt like an attack. Eventually she left. Javier knows he drove her away, but he could not explain it then; he could not explain it now.

What finally brought him to a clinic was a recent incident. A maintenance worker-stocky, male, wearing a gray uniform-walked into a hotel room Javier was cleaning without knocking. Javier saw the uniform out of the corner of his eye and threw his vacuum cleaner at the man, then locked himself in the bathroom for twenty minutes. The hotel did not fire him, but they gave him a written warning. That night, he woke up with his hands around his own throat, gasping. He called a help line the next morning. He does not know if talking will fix anything, but he is terrified of losing this job too, and he is even more terrified of living the rest of his life this way-on edge, alone, and unable to feel anything but fear.
